A.explanation: 1 antinode would mean fewer half-wavelengths fit, which would need a longer wavelength and lower frequency, not a doubled frequency.

B.explanation: 2 antinodes is the original pattern before the frequency is changed, so it ignores the halving of wavelength.

C.explanation: 3 antinodes does not correspond to a whole number of doublings of the original two-loop pattern on the same length of string.

D.explanation: Halving the wavelength doubles the number of half-wavelengths that fit in the fixed length, from 2 to 4, giving 4 antinodes.

hints: Notice the original stationary wave has three nodes and two antinodes on the same stretched string, so the string length $L$ is fixed.
Recall that for a stretched string the wave speed $v$ is fixed, so $v = f\lambda$ means doubling $f$ must halve $\lambda$.
Count how many half-wavelengths $\lambda/2$ fit in $L$ at first, then ask what happens to that count when $\lambda$ is halved and each $\lambda/2$ contains one antinode.
walkthrough: The string length $L$ does not change. The first pattern is node-antinode-node-antinode-node, which is two loops.
One loop is $\lambda/2$, so $L = 2 \times \lambda_1/2 = \lambda_1$ where $\lambda_1$ is the original wavelength.
Wave speed on the string stays the same because tension and mass per unit length are unchanged. Use $v = f\lambda$.
With $v$ constant, doubling $f$ to $2f$ gives $\lambda_2 = v/(2f) = \lambda_1/2$. The new wavelength is half the old wavelength.
Fit the new wavelength into the same length: $L = \lambda_1 = 2\lambda_2 = 4 \times \lambda_2/2$. There are now 4 half-wavelengths.
Each half-wavelength loop contains one antinode, so the new stationary wave has 4 antinodes. This is option D.
